Fluctuation electrodynamics of quantum capacitance in electron bilayers

Dmitry Zverevich Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, Wisconsin 53706, USA    Alberto F. Morpurgo Affiliation: Department of Quantum Matter Physics, University of Geneva, Quai Ernest-Ansermet 24, 1211 Geneva, Switzerland Affiliation: Department of Applied Physics, University of Geneva, 24 Quai Ernest Ansermet, Geneva, CH-1211 Switzerland Affiliation: Geneva Quantum Center, University of Geneva, Switzerland    Alex Levchenko Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, Wisconsin 53706, USA
October 30, 2026
Abstract

Capacitance provides a thermodynamic probe of interacting electrons. It characterizes the energy cost of transferring charge between conductors, which, in low-dimensional systems, is governed by exchange and correlation effects in addition to electrostatic contributions. We develop a theory of the quantum capacitance of electron double layers, semiconductor quantum wells as well as monolayer and bilayer graphene devices, focusing on the contribution generated by interlayer correlations. Within a functional-integral formulation we show that the separation-dependent part of the ground-state energy is, at the level of ring diagrams, exactly the nonretarded Lifshitz expression for the van der Waals energy of two conducting sheets, with reflection amplitudes built from the layer polarizabilities. The interlayer correction to the inverse capacitance is the second density derivative of this energy: a Casimir compressibility. The zero-point fluctuations that generate Casimir forces between mirrors are here the coupled plasmons of the bilayer, and their contribution to the capacitance is obtained in closed form; its sign shows that interlayer correlations oppose charging at high density. A Gell-Mann-Brueckner analysis gives the high-density limit in terms of universal functions. For graphene we find that monolayers behave like the electron gas, while bilayer graphene is anomalous: interband screening suppresses the correction by orders of magnitude and, within the two-band model, can even reverse its sign in the experimentally relevant range of separations. We delineate the limits of the theory, identifying the dilute Wigner-crystal regime and electron-hole double layers near exciton condensation as regimes where the capacitance becomes a probe of interlayer pairing.

I Introduction

Electron double layers, consisting of two conducting sheets separated by a nanometer- to micron-scale insulating barrier that suppresses interlayer tunneling while preserving Coulomb coupling, have long provided a versatile platform for studying electron correlations. Since the two layers are coupled exclusively through the Coulomb forces, any interlayer observable necessarily reflects interaction effects. Coulomb drag, in which a current in one layer transfers momentum to the other, is the transport realization of this idea [1, 2]. Capacitance and penetration-field measurements are its thermodynamic counterpart. Eisenstein et al. [3, 4] showed that the electric field leaking through an imperfectly screening two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) measures the compressibility of that layer. Using a double quantum well, they demonstrated that d​μ/d​nd\mu/dn of a dilute 2DEG is negative, i.e., that exchange and correlation overwhelm the kinetic energy, confirming a prediction made a decade earlier [5, 6].

The graphene era turned these techniques into precision tools. Quantum-capacitance and compressibility measurements on monolayer and bilayer graphene [7, 8, 9, 10, 11], including the dual-gated geometries in which density and layer polarization are tuned independently [12, 13], established capacitance as a spectroscopic probe of band structure and interactions on an equal footing with transport. A number of discoveries have since been made with capacitance bridges: correlated composite-fermion phases in bilayer graphene Landau levels [14], the half- and quarter-metal ferromagnets of rhombohedral trilayer graphene revealed by penetration-field capacitance on graphite-gated van der Waals heterostructures [15], and, most recently, flat-band surface-state superconductivity in thick rhombohedral graphite detected by layer-resolved capacitance [16]. On the theory side these experiments revived interest in the capacitance of interacting double layers [17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24], with particular attention to the dilute regime where the electron liquid is nearly a Wigner crystal and the capacitance can exceed its geometric value [5, 19, 25]. The recent observation of robust Wigner crystals and bilayer Wigner crystals in transition-metal dichalcogenide heterostructures [26, 27, 28, 29] shows that this strongly correlated regime is now accessible experimentally.

An important part of this theory is, however, missing. The measured inverse capacitance of a double layer separates into three parts: the geometric term, the single-layer compressibilities (the conventional “quantum capacitance” [17]), and a remainder generated by correlations between the layers. The single-layer parts are known essentially exactly from quantum Monte Carlo [30, 31]. The interlayer part is the poorly understood one: it has been computed numerically in specific models [22], estimated classically in the Wigner-crystal regime [19], and identified diagrammatically as a “cross quantum capacitance” [23, 24]. Its general structure, controlled limits, asymptotic behavior, and sign have not been established. This is the purpose of the present paper.

The organizing principle of our approach is that this problem belongs to Casimir physics. The Casimir force between conductors [32] and its generalization to real materials, the Lifshitz theory of van der Waals forces [33, 34], express the separation-dependent part of the ground-state energy of two bodies through their electromagnetic reflection amplitudes; the modern state of this field is documented in several monographs [35, 36, 37, 38] and reviews [39]. Casimir-force experiments now operate at separations of 100100 nm–2​μ2\,\mum with sub-percent precision, enough to resolve how the fluctuating fields penetrate real electrodes and to discriminate between models of their low-frequency response [40]. We show that the interlayer correlation energy of an electron bilayer in the ring (random-phase) approximation is the nonretarded Lifshitz energy of two two-dimensional sheets. The reflection amplitude of each sheet is built from its density response function. In the regime relevant to capacitors the zero-point photon modes of the Casimir problem are replaced by the coupled plasma oscillations of the two layers. The interlayer capacitance correction is the second density derivative of their zero-point energy, a quantity we call the Casimir compressibility. The energy part of this correspondence is known in the theory of dispersion forces. Sernelius and Björk computed the van der Waals attraction of two quantum wells [41]; Boström, Sernelius, and earlier Barash found its anomalous fractional power laws [42, 43]; Dobson, White, and Rubio established the corresponding asymptotic benchmarks for layered and graphene systems [44, 45]. The capacitance has not been considered in this context. It requires the dependence of the reflection amplitudes on the layer densities, which is not probed by a Casimir force measured at fixed density. Here we work out these consequences quantitatively for realistic systems. The same interlayer fluctuations, evaluated on the real frequency axis, produce Coulomb drag [2]; the Casimir compressibility is the equilibrium moment of the same fluctuation spectrum, so the present work places drag and capacitance within one framework.

The paper is organized as follows. Section II defines the model, the observables, and the separation of the inverse capacitance into geometric, single-layer, and interlayer parts. Section III derives the interlayer correlation energy from the fermionic functional integral, emphasizing the matrix structure in layer space that distinguishes the bilayer from the textbook single-layer analysis. Section IV proves the equivalence to Lifshitz theory, quantifies the neglect of retardation, discusses finite temperature and the limits of the additive (ring) approximation, and formulates the Casimir compressibility. Section V evaluates the theory for the 2DEG double layer: the exact high-density (Gell-Mann–Brueckner) limit, the ring resummation, the plasmon zero-point asymptotics with their universal constants, and order-of-magnitude estimates (Fig. 1). Section VI presents the corresponding results for monolayer and bilayer graphene (Figs. 2 and 3), including the anomalous sign structure of the bilayer case and the limits of validity near the neutrality point. Section VII places the results against the known limiting regimes, from the classical dipole regime of dilute bilayers to exciton condensation in electron-hole double layers, and identifies the open problems. Section VIII summarizes. Technical material is collected in Appendixes A–C.

II Setup and observables

II.1 Model

We consider two parallel two-dimensional electron layers separated by a distance dd in a uniform dielectric environment ϵ¯\bar{\epsilon} (Gaussian units). Tunneling is absent; the layers are coupled only through the Coulomb interaction. Each layer hosts a translationally invariant electron liquid with areal density nℓn_{\ell} (ℓ=1,2\ell=1,2) on its own neutralizing background, so that each layer is neutral in the reference state. The intra- and interlayer interactions are

v⁡(q)=2​π​e2ϵ¯​q,v12​(q)=2​π​e2ϵ¯​q​e−q​d.v(q)=\frac{2\pi e^{2}}{\bar{\epsilon}q},\qquad v_{12}(q)=\frac{2\pi e^{2}}{\bar{\epsilon}q}\,e^{-qd}. (1)

Three microscopic realizations are treated in parallel: (i) the parabolic 2DEG (mass mm, spin degeneracy 2), for which we use effective atomic units [ℏ=m=e2/ϵ¯=1\hbar=m=e^{2}/\bar{\epsilon}=1, lengths in Bohr radius aB=ϵ¯​ℏ2/m​e2a_{B}=\bar{\epsilon}\hbar^{2}/me^{2}, energies in Hartree unit Ha=e2/ϵ¯​aB\mathrm{Ha}=e^{2}/\bar{\epsilon}a_{B}], with n=kF2/2​πn=k_{F}^{2}/2\pi, density of states ν0=m/π​ℏ2\nu_{0}=m/\pi\hbar^{2}, interaction parameter rs=(πn)−1/2/aBr_{s}=(\pi n)^{-1/2}/a_{B}, and Thomas-Fermi wave vector κ=2​π​e2​ν0/ϵ¯=2/aB\kappa=2\pi e^{2}\nu_{0}/\bar{\epsilon}=2/a_{B}; (ii) doped monolayer graphene (MLG), a chirality-one Dirac liquid with velocity vv, degeneracy g=4g=4, and coupling αg=e2/ϵ¯​ℏ​v\alpha_{\rm g}=e^{2}/\bar{\epsilon}\hbar v; and (iii) doped Bernal bilayer graphene (BLG) in the two-band approximation [46], a chirality-two liquid with mass mm and g=4g=4. For graphene systems n=g​kF2/4​πn=gk_{F}^{2}/4\pi.

II.2 Capacitance as an energy curvature

Let ε⁡(n1,n2,d)\varepsilon(n_{1},n_{2};d) denote the ground-state energy per unit area. Transferring an areal density δ​n\delta n between the plates at fixed total density, n1,2=n¯1,2±δ​nn_{1,2}=\bar{n}_{1,2}\pm\delta n, requires the voltage e​U=∂ε/∂δ​neU=\partial\varepsilon/\partial\delta n, so the differential capacitance per unit area is

1C=1e2​d2​εd​(δ​n)2=1e2​[∂2ε∂n12+∂2ε∂n22−2​∂2ε∂n1​∂n2].\frac{1}{C}=\frac{1}{e^{2}}\frac{d^{2}\varepsilon}{d(\delta n)^{2}}=\frac{1}{e^{2}}\left[\frac{\partial^{2}\varepsilon}{\partial n_{1}^{2}}+\frac{\partial^{2}\varepsilon}{\partial n_{2}^{2}}-2\frac{\partial^{2}\varepsilon}{\partial n_{1}\partial n_{2}}\right]. (2)

Equation (2) agrees with the curvature formula used in Ref. [22] and, in linear-response language, with the general result of Ref. [23]. The energy separates into three distinct contributions,

ε=2​π​e2​dϵ¯​δ​n2+ε0​(n1)+ε0​(n2)+εint​(n1,n2,d),\varepsilon=\frac{2\pi e^{2}d}{\bar{\epsilon}}\,\delta n^{2}+\varepsilon_{0}(n_{1})+\varepsilon_{0}(n_{2})+\varepsilon_{\rm int}(n_{1},n_{2};d), (3)

namely the electrostatic (Hartree) energy of the transferred charge, the energies of the two isolated layers, and the interlayer correlation energy, which contains all the dd dependence beyond electrostatics. Here ε0​(n)\varepsilon_{0}(n) is the ground-state energy per unit area of an isolated neutral layer of density nn on its own neutralizing background, so that μ0​(n)=d​ε0/d​n\mu_{0}(n)=d\varepsilon_{0}/dn below is the standard chemical potential of the two-dimensional electron liquid. The entire electrostatic energy of the transferred charge is contained in the first term, which is exact for uniform sheets; the exchange-correlation energy of a uniform layer does not depend on where its neutralizing charge resides, so defining ε0\varepsilon_{0} instead at a fixed background would differ from our convention only by that Hartree term. Accordingly,

C−1=4​π​dϵ¯+1e2​[∂μ0∂n|n1+∂μ0∂n|n2]+δ​Cinter−1,\displaystyle C^{-1}=\frac{4\pi d}{\bar{\epsilon}}+\frac{1}{e^{2}}\left[\frac{\partial\mu_{0}}{\partial n}\Big|_{n_{1}}+\frac{\partial\mu_{0}}{\partial n}\Big|_{n_{2}}\right]+\delta C^{-1}_{\rm inter}, (4)
δCinter−1≡1e2[∂n12+∂n22−2∂n1∂n2]εint.\displaystyle\delta C^{-1}_{\rm inter}\equiv\frac{1}{e^{2}}\Bigl[\partial^{2}_{n_{1}}+\partial^{2}_{n_{2}}-2\,\partial_{n_{1}}\partial_{n_{2}}\Bigr]\,\varepsilon_{\rm int}. (5)

The first term of Eq. (4) is the geometric capacitance; the second contains the single-layer inverse compressibilities, negative at low density [5, 3, 4] and known essentially exactly from quantum Monte Carlo parametrizations [30, 31, 47]. The third term is the subject of this paper. The derivatives in Eqs. (4) and (5) are evaluated at the actual layer densities n1,2=n¯±δ​nn_{1,2}=\bar{n}\pm\delta n of the biased state; Eq. (4) is the differential capacitance at that working point. For a symmetric device at zero bias both arguments equal n¯\bar{n}, which is the case evaluated in Secs. V and VI.

Two remarks about this separation are in order. First, Eq. (3) defines ε0​(n)\varepsilon_{0}(n) as the energy of an isolated layer: since the dielectric environment is uniform, the intralayer interaction carries no dependence on dd, and every interlayer effect, including the modification of intralayer screening by the presence of the second layer, resides, by construction, in εint\varepsilon_{\rm int}. This convention differs from analyses formulated in terms of the polarizabilities of the coupled capacitor [23]. There the “intralayer” response Πℓ​ℓ\Pi_{\ell\ell} is itself dressed by the other plate, and only the off-diagonal Π12\Pi_{12} is counted as a cross term. The two conventions are related by moving the diagonal derivatives ∂2εint/∂nℓ2\partial^{2}\varepsilon_{\rm int}/\partial n_{\ell}^{2}, the dd-dependent renormalization of each layer’s compressibility, from one category to the other. The quantities that do not depend on the convention are εint\varepsilon_{\rm int} and its full Hessian, which is what we compute. As shown in Sec. V.3, the diagonal part carries about two thirds of the interlayer correction and the pure cross part one third; identifying the interlayer effect with the cross term alone would therefore understate it substantially. Second, it is convenient to quote the interlayer correction as a shift of the effective capacitor thickness d∗≡ϵ¯/4​π​Cd^{*}\equiv\bar{\epsilon}/4\pi C,

δ​dinter∗=ϵ¯4​π​δ​Cinter−1.\delta d^{*}_{\rm inter}=\frac{\bar{\epsilon}}{4\pi}\,\delta C^{-1}_{\rm inter}. (6)

We note that the full Hessian ∂μi/∂nj\partial\mu_{i}/\partial n_{j} also controls the penetration-field capacitance and the Eisenstein ratio [3, 13, 22]; measuring several capacitances of one device therefore separates the mixed derivative ∂n1∂n2ε\partial_{n_{1}}\partial_{n_{2}}\varepsilon from the diagonal terms, a point we return to in Sec. VII.

III Interlayer correlation energy from the functional integral

III.1 Partition function and layer-space structure

We start from the imaginary-time coherent-state representation of the grand partition function,

Z=∫D⁡[ψ¯,ψ]​e−S⁡[ψ¯,ψ],S=S0+Sint,Z=\int D[\bar{\psi},\psi]\,e^{-S[\bar{\psi},\psi]},\qquad S=S_{0}+S_{\rm int}, (7)

with the free action

S0=∫0βdτ∑ℓ=1,2∑𝒌ψ¯ℓ​𝒌(∂τ+ξℓ​𝒌)ψℓ​𝒌,S_{0}=\int_{0}^{\beta}\!d\tau\sum_{\ell=1,2}\sum_{\bm{k}}\bar{\psi}_{\ell\bm{k}}\bigl(\partial_{\tau}+\xi_{\ell\bm{k}}\bigr)\psi_{\ell\bm{k}}, (8)

where ξℓ​𝒌\xi_{\ell\bm{k}} is the band dispersion of layer ℓ\ell measured from its chemical potential (band and spin indices are implicit), and the density-density interaction

Sint=12​𝒜​∫0βd​τ​∑𝒒≠0∑ℓ​ℓ′ρℓ,−𝒒​Vℓ​ℓ′​(q)​ρℓ′,𝒒,\displaystyle S_{\rm int}=\frac{1}{2\mathcal{A}}\int_{0}^{\beta}\!d\tau\sum_{\bm{q}\neq 0}\sum_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\rho_{\ell,-\bm{q}}\,V_{\ell\ell^{\prime}}(q)\,\rho_{\ell^{\prime},\bm{q}}, (9a)
V^​(q)=(vv12v12v).\displaystyle\hat{V}(q)=\begin{pmatrix}v&v_{12}\\ v_{12}&v\end{pmatrix}. (9b)

Here ρℓ,𝒒=∑𝒌ψ¯ℓ,𝒌​ψℓ,𝒌+𝒒\rho_{\ell,\bm{q}}=\sum_{\bm{k}}\bar{\psi}_{\ell,\bm{k}}\psi_{\ell,\bm{k}+\bm{q}} and the 𝒒=0\bm{q}=0 component is cancelled by the neutralizing backgrounds. The only difference from the single-layer problem is that the interaction is a 2×22\times 2 matrix in layer space, with the entire dd dependence residing in the off-diagonal element v12​(q)=v⁡(q)​e−q​dv_{12}(q)=v(q)e^{-qd} of Eq. (1). Since the layers are distinguishable and tunneling is absent, there are no interlayer Green’s functions: interlayer exchange vanishes identically, and the interlayer energy starts at second order in v12v_{12} (it is pure correlation). This removes the second-order exchange term that complicates the original Gell-Mann-Brueckner analysis of the bulk electron gas [48]. The matrix V^​(q)\hat{V}(q) is invertible for any d>0d>0, detV^=v2​(1−e−2​q​d)\det\hat{V}=v^{2}(1-e^{-2qd}), so a Hubbard-Stratonovich decoupling in the charge channel is well defined.

Introducing a two-component real bosonic field ϕℓ​(𝒒,τ)\phi_{\ell}(\bm{q},\tau) conjugate to the layer densities and decoupling Eq. (9),

Z=∫Dϕe−12∫ϕTV^−1ϕ∫D[ψ¯,ψ]e−∑ℓψ¯ℓ(G^−10​ℓ+iϕℓ)ψℓ,Z=\int D\phi\;e^{-\frac{1}{2}\int\phi^{T}\hat{V}^{-1}\phi}\int D[\bar{\psi},\psi]\,e^{-\sum_{\ell}\bar{\psi}_{\ell}(\hat{G}^{-1}_{0\ell}+i\phi_{\ell})\psi_{\ell}}, (10)

the fermions appear quadratically and can be integrated out exactly:

Z=∫Dϕexp{−12∫ϕTV^−1ϕ+∑ℓTrln[G^0​ℓ−1+iϕℓ]}.Z=\int D\phi\;\exp\Bigl\{-\tfrac{1}{2}\!\int\!\phi^{T}\hat{V}^{-1}\phi+\sum_{\ell}\mathrm{Tr}\ln\bigl[\hat{G}^{-1}_{0\ell}+i\phi_{\ell}\bigr]\Bigr\}. (11)

The Tr​ln\mathrm{Tr}\ln is diagonal in the layer index (each fermion couples only to its own field ϕℓ\phi_{\ell}) while the fields are coupled through V^−1\hat{V}^{-1}. All interlayer physics is therefore mediated by the boson propagator, i.e., by the screened Coulomb interaction; this is the formal statement of the absence of interlayer exchange.

III.2 One-loop free energy

Expanding the Tr​ln\mathrm{Tr}\ln in Eq. (11) to quadratic order in ϕℓ\phi_{\ell} generates 12​ϕT​χ^0​ϕ\frac{1}{2}\phi^{T}\hat{\chi}_{0}\phi, with χ^0=diag⁡(χ0,1,χ0,2)\hat{\chi}_{0}=\mathrm{diag}(\chi_{0,1},\chi_{0,2}) the matrix of free polarization bubbles, χ0,ℓ​(q,i​Ωm)<0\chi_{0,\ell}(q,i\Omega_{m})<0 on the Matsubara axis. The remaining Gaussian integral gives the fluctuation grand potential per unit area

Δ​Ω𝒜=12​β​∑Ωm∫d2​q(2​π)2​ln​det[𝟙−V^​(q)​χ^0​(q,i​Ωm)]+⋯,\frac{\Delta\Omega}{\mathcal{A}}=\frac{1}{2\beta}\sum_{\Omega_{m}}\int\!\frac{d^{2}q}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,\ln\det\bigl[\mathbbm{1}-\hat{V}(q)\hat{\chi}_{0}(q,i\Omega_{m})\bigr]+\;\cdots, (12)

where the ellipsis denotes normal-ordering constants that are linear in the layer densities nℓn_{\ell} and are therefore annihilated by the second derivatives in Eq. (2). Equation (12) is the bilayer generalization of the familiar ring (RPA) exchange-correlation energy; the only difference is the determinant over the layer space,

det[𝟙−V^​χ^0]=(1−v​χ0,1)​(1−v​χ0,2)−v122​χ0,1​χ0,2.\det\bigl[\mathbbm{1}-\hat{V}\hat{\chi}_{0}\bigr]=(1-v\chi_{0,1})(1-v\chi_{0,2})-v_{12}^{2}\,\chi_{0,1}\chi_{0,2}. (13)

At T→0T\to 0, β−1∑Ωm→∫−∞∞dξ/2π\beta^{-1}\sum_{\Omega_{m}}\to\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}d\xi/2\pi. Subtracting the isolated-layer logarithms, which renormalize ε0​(nℓ)\varepsilon_{0}(n_{\ell}) in Eq. (3), the interlayer part (the only dd-dependent part) takes the compact form

Eint𝒜\displaystyle\frac{E_{\rm int}}{\mathcal{A}} =ℏ2​∫d2​q(2​π)2​∫−∞∞d​ξ2​π​ln⁡[1−v122​χ0,1​χ0,2(1−v​χ0,1)​(1−v​χ0,2)]\displaystyle=\frac{\hbar}{2}\int\!\frac{d^{2}q}{(2\pi)^{2}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\frac{d\xi}{2\pi}\,\ln\left[1-\frac{v_{12}^{2}\,\chi_{0,1}\chi_{0,2}}{(1-v\chi_{0,1})(1-v\chi_{0,2})}\right]
=ℏ2​∫d2​q(2​π)2​∫−∞∞d​ξ2​π​ln⁡[1−e−2​q​d​r1​r2],\displaystyle=\frac{\hbar}{2}\int\!\frac{d^{2}q}{(2\pi)^{2}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\frac{d\xi}{2\pi}\,\ln\bigl[1-e^{-2qd}\,r_{1}r_{2}\bigr], (14)

where

rℓ​(q,i​ξ)=v⁡(q)​χ0,ℓ​(q,i​ξ)1−v⁡(q)​χ0,ℓ​(q,i​ξ)∈(−1,0).r_{\ell}(q,i\xi)=\frac{v(q)\,\chi_{0,\ell}(q,i\xi)}{1-v(q)\,\chi_{0,\ell}(q,i\xi)}\;\in(-1,0). (15)

Here χ0,ℓ\chi_{0,\ell} is the bare bubble, i.e., the proper (irreducible) polarizability of layer ℓ\ell at the RPA level, and the denominator 1−v​χ0,ℓ1-v\chi_{0,\ell} generates the intralayer screening. Beyond RPA, the quantity entering Eq. (15) is the proper polarizability Π~ℓ\tilde{\Pi}_{\ell} of the isolated layer, which includes the intralayer local-field (vertex) corrections; equivalently, rℓ=v​χℓr_{\ell}=v\chi_{\ell} with χℓ=Π~ℓ/(1−v​Π~ℓ)\chi_{\ell}=\tilde{\Pi}_{\ell}/(1-v\tilde{\Pi}_{\ell}) the full density response of the isolated layer. Inserting the full response into Eq. (15) would count the intralayer screening twice. Equation (14), together with the capacitance formula (2), is the principal result of this section: it is negative (interlayer attraction), vanishes as d→∞d\to\infty, and its density Hessian yields δ​Cinter−1\delta C^{-1}_{\rm inter}. Replacing the bare bubbles χ0,ℓ\chi_{0,\ell} by the proper polarizabilities Π~ℓ\tilde{\Pi}_{\ell} of the isolated layers extends Eq. (14) to the additive approximation discussed in the next section; corrections to it are diagrams in which interlayer interaction lines attach to a common vertex, interlayer ladders, whose physical content is excitonic and whose role is examined in Secs. VI.4 and VII.

IV Equivalence to the Lifshitz theory and the Casimir compressibility

IV.1 The identification argument

The zero-temperature, nonretarded Lifshitz energy of two bodies facing each other across a gap dd, with specular reflection amplitudes r1,2​(q,i​ξ)r_{1,2}(q,i\xi) for evanescent waves of in-plane momentum qq, is precisely of the form (14) [33, 35, 39]. The identification is completed by showing that Eq. (15) is the electrostatic reflection amplitude of a strictly two-dimensional conducting sheet. Place the sheet at z=0z=0 and apply an external evanescent potential ϕext=ϕ0​ei​q​x​eq​z\phi_{\rm ext}=\phi_{0}\,e^{iqx}e^{qz} incident from z<0z<0. The sheet develops the induced density δ​n=χ​ϕtot​(0)\delta n=\chi\,\phi_{\rm tot}(0), which radiates the potential ϕind=v⁡(q)​δ​n​e−q​|z|\phi_{\rm ind}=v(q)\,\delta n\,e^{-q|z|}. Solving the self-consistency condition at z=0z=0 gives ϕtot​(0)=ϕ0/(1−v​χ)\phi_{\rm tot}(0)=\phi_{0}/(1-v\chi) and hence the reflected amplitude

r⁡(q,i​ξ)=ϕindϕ0|z=0=v⁡(q)​χ​(q,i​ξ)1−v⁡(q)​χ​(q,i​ξ),r(q,i\xi)=\frac{\phi_{\rm ind}}{\phi_{0}}\Big|_{z=0}=\frac{v(q)\chi(q,i\xi)}{1-v(q)\chi(q,i\xi)}, (16)

which is Eq. (15). The response function χ\chi in this argument is defined with respect to the total potential at the sheet and is therefore the proper polarizability; in terms of the full response χfull=χ/(1−v​χ)\chi^{\rm full}=\chi/(1-v\chi) to the external potential, Eq. (16) reads simply r=v​χfullr=v\chi^{\rm full}. A perfect metal corresponds to r=−1r=-1, i.e., χfull→−1/v\chi^{\rm full}\to-1/v; a weakly polarizable sheet to r≃v​χr\simeq v\chi. Thus the interlayer part of the bilayer ground-state energy is the van der Waals-Casimir energy of the two sheets, and the interlayer contribution to the inverse capacitance, Eq. (5), is its second density derivative—a Casimir compressibility.

Capacitance measurements on double layers therefore probe a dispersion force thermodynamically: Casimir experiments measure the force −∂dEint-\partial_{d}E_{\rm int} [40, 39], while a capacitance bridge measures the second derivative ∂δ​n2Eint\partial^{2}_{\delta n}E_{\rm int} of the same energy with respect to the transferred charge.

IV.2 Domain of validity of the correspondence

Three qualifications define where Eq. (14) applies.

(i) Retardation. The full Lifshitz theory replaces the electrostatic kernel e−2​q​de^{-2qd} by photon propagators; Eq. (14) is its c→∞c\to\infty limit. The nonretarded form holds while the relevant fluctuation frequencies, ξ∼ωp​(q∼1/d)\xi\sim\omega_{p}(q\sim 1/d) with ωp​(q)=(2​π​n​e2​q/m​ϵ¯)1/2\omega_{p}(q)=(2\pi ne^{2}q/m\bar{\epsilon})^{1/2} the two-dimensional plasmon, remain small compared with the photon frequency c​qcq at the dominant momenta, ωp​(1/d)≪c/d\omega_{p}(1/d)\ll c/d. This condition fails only at separations d≳c2​m​ϵ¯/2​π​n​e2d\gtrsim c^{2}m\bar{\epsilon}/2\pi ne^{2}, which is macroscopic (fractions of a millimeter and beyond) for all realistic densities; the crossover to the true Casimir regime for two-dimensional sheets was mapped in Ref. [41]. Capacitors are therefore always in the nonretarded regime, which is why plasmons, rather than photons, play the role of the fluctuating modes here.

(ii) Finite temperature. At T>0T>0 the frequency integral becomes a Matsubara sum and Eq. (12) already has the required form. The Ωm=0\Omega_{m}=0 term is the classical (static) fluctuation attraction; its growing relative weight at high temperature is the bilayer analog of the thermal Casimir force. All results below are at T=0T=0.

(iii) Additivity. Lifshitz theory takes the response of each body as given. Diagrammatically, Eq. (14) with the exact proper polarizabilities Π~ℓ\tilde{\Pi}_{\ell} of the isolated layers resums all diagrams in which the interlayer lines connect closed polarization loops; it omits interlayer vertex corrections (particle-particle ladders), whose physical content is interlayer exciton formation. These are negligible at high density and weak interlayer coupling, but dominate in dilute bilayers and in electron-hole double layers near exciton condensation, the same non-additivity that limits Lifshitz theory for atomically close or chemically interacting surfaces [39].

IV.3 Relation to Coulomb drag

The building blocks of Eq. (14), the screened interlayer interaction and the two polarization functions, are exactly those of the Coulomb drag transresistivity [2, 49]. Drag is determined by the dissipative part of the interlayer fluctuation spectrum: it involves Im​χ1​Im​χ2\mathrm{Im}\,\chi_{1}\,\mathrm{Im}\,\chi_{2} at real frequencies, weighted by a thermal factor. The Casimir compressibility is determined by the reactive part of the same spectrum, an integral of the coupled response over imaginary frequencies. The two observables thus probe the same interlayer coupling, one out of equilibrium and the other in equilibrium. This suggests quantitative cross-checks between drag and capacitance data on the same device, a point developed in Sec. VII.

V Two-dimensional electron gas double layer

Throughout this section the layers are identical unpolarized 2DEGs and we use effective atomic units. The Lindhard function on the imaginary axis has the closed form [Appendix A]

χ0​(q,i​ξ)=−ν0​[1−1b​Re​(b+i​a)2−1],\chi_{0}(q,i\xi)=-\nu_{0}\Bigl[1-\tfrac{1}{b}\,\mathrm{Re}\sqrt{(b+ia)^{2}-1}\Bigr], (17)

with the dimensionless variables b=q/2​kFb=q/2k_{F} and a=ξ/q​vFa=\xi/qv_{F}.

V.1 High-density limit: a Gell-Mann-Brueckner analysis

Expanding Eq. (14) to second order in v12v_{12} with bare bubbles gives the leading interlayer term of the high-density expansion,

E2𝒜=−ℏ2∫d2​q(2​π)2v122(q)∫−∞+∞d​ξ2​πχ0,1χ0,2.\frac{E_{2}}{\mathcal{A}}=-\frac{\hbar}{2}\int\!\frac{d^{2}q}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,v_{12}^{2}(q)\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\frac{d\xi}{2\pi}\,\chi_{0,1}\chi_{0,2}. (18)

In the bulk electron gas the analogous second-order term diverges in the infrared and forces the Gell-Mann–Brueckner ring resummation [48]; in two dimensions the single-layer second order is already finite [50], and the interlayer term (18) is finite as well: the frequency integral supplies a factor ∝q\propto q at small qq, ∫0∞d​ξ​[1−ξ/ξ2+vF2​q2]2=(2−π2)​vF​q\int_{0}^{\infty}d\xi\,[1-\xi/\sqrt{\xi^{2}+v_{F}^{2}q^{2}}]^{2}=(2-\tfrac{\pi}{2})v_{F}q, so the momentum integrand is regular. The high-density expansion therefore terminates at second order; the ring resummation is needed only when screening is strong (Sec. V.2). Moreover, because interlayer exchange is absent (Sec. III), Eq. (18) is the complete leading term.

Scaling out the density, Eq. (18) defines universal functions of the single variable x=kF​dx=k_{F}d:

E2N=−2π​G​(x)​Ha,δ​C2−1=H⁡(x)e2​n,\frac{E_{2}}{N}=-\frac{2}{\pi}G(x)~\text{Ha},\qquad\delta C^{-1}_{2}=\frac{H(x)}{e^{2}n}, (19)

where N=n​𝒜N=n\mathcal{A} is the electron number of one layer [per unit area, E2/𝒜=−(2/π)​n​G​(x)E_{2}/\mathcal{A}=-(2/\pi)\,nG(x) Ha]. Normalized per particle, the energy carries no residual rsr_{s} dependence in absolute units, the bilayer counterpart of the Gell-Mann-Brueckner constant. Explicitly, with f⁡(b,a)=1−Re​(b+i​a)2−1/bf(b,a)=1-\mathrm{Re}\sqrt{(b+ia)^{2}-1}/b the dimensionless Lindhard function of Eq. (17), χ0=−f/π\chi_{0}=-f/\pi, and ∂n=(π/kF)∂kF\partial_{n}=(\pi/k_{F})\partial_{k_{F}} acting on χ0\chi_{0} through bb and aa,

G⁡(x)\displaystyle G(x) =2​∫0∞d​b​e−4​x​b​∫0∞d​a​f2​(b,a),\displaystyle=2\int_{0}^{\infty}\!db\,e^{-4xb}\!\int_{0}^{\infty}\!da\,f^{2}(b,a),
H⁡(x)\displaystyle H(x) =−n∫d2​q(2​π)2v122(q)∫−∞∞d​ξ2​π[χ0∂n2χ0−(∂nχ0)2],\displaystyle=-n\!\int\!\frac{d^{2}q}{(2\pi)^{2}}\,v_{12}^{2}(q)\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\!\frac{d\xi}{2\pi}\,\bigl[\chi_{0}\,\partial_{n}^{2}\chi_{0}-(\partial_{n}\chi_{0})^{2}\bigr], (20)

the latter evaluated at n1=n2=nn_{1}=n_{2}=n in effective atomic units; both depend on kF​dk_{F}d only. Numerically G⁡(0)=0.964G(0)=0.964, and since f⁡(0,a)=1−a/1+a2f(0,a)=1-a/\sqrt{1+a^{2}} the tails are G⁡(x)→(2−π/2)/2​xG(x)\to(2-\pi/2)/2x [equivalently E2/𝒜→−(2−π2)e4ν02vF/2dE_{2}/\mathcal{A}\to-(2-\tfrac{\pi}{2})e^{4}\nu_{0}^{2}v_{F}/2d] and H⁡(x)≃0.097/xH(x)\simeq 0.097/x, and H⁡(x)>0H(x)>0 everywhere: already at second order, interlayer correlations reduce the capacitance at high density. In terms of the effective thickness, δ​d2∗=rs24​H​(kF​d)​aB\delta d^{*}_{2}=\tfrac{r_{s}^{2}}{4}H(k_{F}d)\,a_{B}.

V.2 Ring resummation and plasmon zero-point energy

At fixed kF​dk_{F}d the parameter controlling successive rings is κ​d=2​rs​(kF​d)\kappa d=\sqrt{2}\,r_{s}(k_{F}d). For κ​d≳1\kappa d\gtrsim 1 the full logarithm of Eq. (14) must be kept, and screening converts the bare 1/d1/d tail of E2E_{2} into a much faster decay. For κ​d≫1\kappa d\gg 1 the integral is dominated by q∼1/2​d≪{κ,kF}q\sim 1/2d\ll\{\kappa,k_{F}\}, where r(q,iξ)≃−ωp2(q)/[ωp2(q)+ξ2]r(q,i\xi)\simeq-\omega_{p}^{2}(q)/[\omega_{p}^{2}(q)+\xi^{2}] with ωp2​(q)=2​π​n​e2​q/m​ϵ¯\omega_{p}^{2}(q)=2\pi ne^{2}q/m\bar{\epsilon}. The frequency integral is then elementary and Eq. (14) becomes the change in zero-point energy of the coupled optical and acoustic plasmons of the bilayer,

Eint𝒜=ℏ4​π​∫0∞d​q​q​[ω+​(q)+ω−​(q)−2​ωp​(q)],\frac{E_{\rm int}}{\mathcal{A}}=\frac{\hbar}{4\pi}\int_{0}^{\infty}\!dq\,q\bigl[\omega_{+}(q)+\omega_{-}(q)-2\omega_{p}(q)\bigr], (21)

with ω±=ωp​1±e−q​d\omega_{\pm}=\omega_{p}\sqrt{1\pm e^{-qd}}. Equation (21) makes the analogy with the Casimir effect explicit: the photon modes of the metallic Casimir problem are replaced by the two-dimensional plasmons. Substituting u=q​du=qd,

Eint𝒜=ℏ4​π​2​π​n​e2m​ϵ¯​Jd5/2,J=−0.0629780,\frac{E_{\rm int}}{\mathcal{A}}=\frac{\hbar}{4\pi}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi ne^{2}}{m\bar{\epsilon}}}\,\frac{J}{d^{5/2}},\quad J=-0.0629780, (22)

where J=∫0∞d​u​u3/2​[1+e−u+1−e−u−2]J=\int_{0}^{\infty}du\,u^{3/2}[\sqrt{1+e^{-u}}+\sqrt{1-e^{-u}}-2] admits the rapidly convergent series J=3​π2∑k≥1(1/22​k)(2k)−5/2J=\tfrac{3\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\sum_{k\geq 1}\binom{1/2}{2k}(2k)^{-5/2} [Appendix B].

This d−5/2d^{-5/2} law is the fractional-power van der Waals attraction of two-dimensional metals known from the theory of dispersion forces. Equation (22) reproduces, including the coefficient, the numerical result of Sernelius and Björk for a pair of quantum wells, E≃−0.012 562eℏn/ϵ¯​m∗d−5/2E\simeq-0.012\,562\,e\hbar\sqrt{n/\bar{\epsilon}m^{*}}\,d^{-5/2} [41], since |J|​2​π/4​π=0.012 563|J|\sqrt{2\pi}/4\pi=0.012\,563. The fractional powers of thin metallic films were analyzed in Refs. [43, 42], and Dobson, White, and Rubio established d−5/2d^{-5/2} (two-dimensional metals) and d−3d^{-3} (undoped graphene) as analytic benchmarks that pairwise-additive van der Waals functionals fail to reproduce [44]; the graphene case at RPA level was studied in Ref. [45]. Figure 1 (left) shows the full evaluation of Eq. (14) with the exact Lindhard function crossing over from the second-order 1/d1/d behavior at κ​d≲1\kappa d\lesssim 1 to the plasmon law (22), which it approaches to within 2%2\% by kF​d≃30k_{F}d\simeq 30.

V.3 Capacitance correction: closed asymptote, sign, decomposition

Differentiating Eq. (21) at fixed total density, with ωp,ℓ2∝q​nℓ\omega^{2}_{p,\ell}\propto q\,n_{\ell}, gives the central quantitative result for parabolic layers [Appendix B]:

δ​Cinter−1=ℏ4​π​e2​n2​2​π​n​e2m​ϵ¯​Kd5/2,K=+0.0477118,\delta C^{-1}_{\rm inter}=\frac{\hbar}{4\pi e^{2}n^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{2\pi ne^{2}}{m\bar{\epsilon}}}\,\frac{K}{d^{5/2}},\qquad K=+0.0477118, (23)

where K=∫0∞d​u​u3/2​D​(e−u)K=\int_{0}^{\infty}du\,u^{3/2}D(e^{-u}) with

D⁡(a)=12−1−a21+a+1−a=316​a2+17256​a4+…D(a)=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\sqrt{1-a^{2}}}{\sqrt{1+a}+\sqrt{1-a}}=\frac{3}{16}a^{2}+\frac{17}{256}a^{4}+\dots (24)

The compact form of DD makes the sign manifest: since 1−a2=(1+a)​(1−a)\sqrt{1-a^{2}}=\sqrt{(1+a)(1-a)}, the arithmetic–geometric-mean inequality gives D⁡(a)≥0D(a)\geq 0 on 0≤a≤10\leq a\leq 1. Throughout the high-density regime, interlayer ring correlations increase 1/C1/C: the van der Waals binding of the layers is maximal at equal densities, so transferring charge costs correlation energy and opposes charging. (The curvature integrand and its numerically stable form are derived in Appendix B; quadrature details are given in Appendix C.) In dimensionless variables,

δ​dinter∗≃0.01​rs(kF​d)5/2​aB,κ​d≫1.\delta d^{*}_{\rm inter}\simeq 0.01\,\frac{\sqrt{r_{s}}}{(k_{F}d)^{5/2}}\;a_{B},\qquad\kappa d\gg 1. (25)

Equations (22) and (23) are two derivatives of the same functional, and in the plasmon regime they are related directly. Both scale as d−5/2d^{-5/2}, so the attractive Casimir pressure between the layers, PC≡|∂dEint|/𝒜=52​|Eint|/𝒜​dP_{C}\equiv|\partial_{d}E_{\rm int}|/\mathcal{A}=\tfrac{5}{2}|E_{\rm int}|/\mathcal{A}d, determines the capacitance correction with a universal coefficient,

δ​Cinter−1=K|J|​|Eint|𝒜​e2​n2=2​K5​|J|​d​PCe2​n2,2​K5​|J|=0.303.\delta C^{-1}_{\rm inter}=\frac{K}{|J|}\,\frac{|E_{\rm int}|}{\mathcal{A}\,e^{2}n^{2}}=\frac{2K}{5|J|}\,\frac{d\,P_{C}}{e^{2}n^{2}},\qquad\frac{2K}{5|J|}=0.303. (26)

The same relation holds for Dirac layers with K→K1/2K\to K_{1/2} [2​K1/2/5​|J|=0.1262K_{1/2}/5|J|=0.126; Sec. VI.2]. Equation (26) shows in what sense a capacitance measures the same dispersion force as a Casimir experiment: when the plasmon zero-point motion dominates, the Casimir pressure determines the interlayer capacitance correction, and vice versa, without free parameters. Away from this regime the two observables remain derivatives of the single functional of Eq. (14), but no closed relation between them exists. The full ring evaluation converges onto Eq. (23) [ratio 0.940.94 at kF​d=28k_{F}d=28, 0.990.99 at kF​d=113k_{F}d=113; Fig. 1, right]. The decomposition of the curvature is instructive: the mixed-derivative (“cross”) part −2∂n1∂n2εint-2\partial_{n_{1}}\partial_{n_{2}}\varepsilon_{\rm int} contributes the fraction 0.3350.335 of Eq. (23), essentially independent of dd and rsr_{s} (the plasmon-pole model gives 0.33450.3345 analytically, and exactly 13\tfrac{1}{3} at leading order in e−q​de^{-qd}). The remaining two thirds is the dd-dependent renormalization of each layer’s compressibility by the presence of the other layer.

To estimate the magnitude: in GaAs double quantum wells (aB≃10a_{B}\simeq 10 nm, rs≃2r_{s}\simeq 2, d≃30d\simeq 30 nm, kF​d≃2k_{F}d\simeq 2) the second-order estimate gives δ​d∗∼rs24​H​(2)≃0.05​aB≃0.5\delta d^{*}\sim\tfrac{r_{s}^{2}}{4}H(2)\simeq 0.05\,a_{B}\simeq 0.5 nm, reduced further by screening toward Eq. (25), a percent-level, density- and separation-dependent correction to d∗d^{*}, distinguishable from the geometric term (∝d\propto d, density independent) and from the single-layer compressibility terms (dd independent) by its n−3/2d−5/2n^{-3/2}d^{-5/2} signature.

The second-order functions GG and HH are controlled for rs≪1r_{s}\ll 1. The large-separation asymptotes, Eqs. (22), (23), and (26), are exact beyond the ring approximation at leading order in 1/κ​d1/\kappa d, for any rsr_{s} at which the layer is a Fermi liquid: for κ​d≫1\kappa d\gg 1 the integral is dominated by q≪kFq\ll k_{F} and ξ∼ωp≫vF​q\xi\sim\omega_{p}\gg v_{F}q, where the proper polarizability of a parabolic layer is fixed by the ff-sum rule, Π~→−nq2/mξ2\tilde{\Pi}\to-nq^{2}/m\xi^{2}, so that the reflection amplitude reduces to the exact long-wavelength plasmon pole and the constants JJ and KK do not depend on the approximation used for the layer response; rsr_{s} enters only through the prefactor n\sqrt{n}. The ring approximation is used at RPA accuracy only in the crossover region κ​d∼1\kappa d\sim 1 and in the rate of approach to the asymptote. There the omitted intralayer local-field corrections to Π~\tilde{\Pi} are of relative order Glf​(q∼1/d)∼1/kF​dG_{\rm lf}(q\sim 1/d)\sim 1/k_{F}d, where Glf​(q)G_{\rm lf}(q) is the static local-field factor of the layer, which vanishes linearly as q→0q\to 0. The value rs=4r_{s}=4 in Fig. 1 was chosen so that the crossover at κ​d=1\kappa d=1 and the asymptotic regime both fall in the plotted window; the curves illustrate the crossover at the RPA level.

VI Graphene double layers

We now evaluate the theory for doped MLG and BLG double layers using the full dynamical polarizabilities. Band models: MLG, ε±​(k)=±ℏ​v​k\varepsilon_{\pm}(k)=\pm\hbar vk, chirality J=1J=1; BLG, the two-band model [46], ε±(k)=±ℏ2k2/2m\varepsilon_{\pm}(k)=\pm\hbar^{2}k^{2}/2m, J=2J=2; coherence factors Fs​s′​(𝒌,𝒌′)=12​[1+s​s′​cos⁡J​φ𝒌​𝒌′]F_{ss^{\prime}}(\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime})=\tfrac{1}{2}[1+ss^{\prime}\cos J\varphi_{\bm{k}\bm{k}^{\prime}}], g=4g=4. Reference parameters: αg=0.5\alpha_{\rm g}=0.5 (hBN encapsulation) for MLG; kF​aB∗=1.25k_{F}a_{B}^{*}=1.25 for BLG (aB∗=ϵ¯​ℏ2/m​e2≃7a_{B}^{*}=\bar{\epsilon}\hbar^{2}/me^{2}\simeq 7 nm for m=0.033​m0m=0.033m_{0}, ϵ¯=4.4\bar{\epsilon}=4.4), corresponding to n=1012n=10^{12} cm-2, kF=0.177k_{F}=0.177 nm-1.

VI.1 Polarizabilities for MLG and BLG devices

The dynamical polarizabilities of doped MLG and BLG are available in closed form [51, 52, 53, 54, 55] and underlie the Coulomb-drag theory of these systems [49]. The published expressions are lengthy and piecewise and do not allow analytical progress. We therefore compute the T=0T=0 imaginary-axis bubbles directly from the band models 11 1 In this subsection we set ℏ=1\hbar=1, so that the imaginary frequency ξ\xi is measured in energy units.,

Π⁡(q,i​ξ)\displaystyle\Pi(q,i\xi) =Πvac​(q,i​ξ)\displaystyle=\Pi_{\rm vac}(q,i\xi)
+g∑s′=±∫k<kFd2​k(2​π)2F+s′(𝒌,𝒌+𝒒)2​Δs′ξ2+Δs′2,\displaystyle+g\sum_{s^{\prime}=\pm}\int_{k<k_{F}}\!\!\frac{d^{2}k}{(2\pi)^{2}}F_{+s^{\prime}}(\bm{k},\bm{k}+\bm{q})\,\frac{2\Delta_{s^{\prime}}}{\xi^{2}+\Delta_{s^{\prime}}^{2}}, (27)

Δs′=ε+​(k)−εs′​(|𝒌+𝒒|)\Delta_{s^{\prime}}=\varepsilon_{+}(k)-\varepsilon_{s^{\prime}}(|\bm{k}+\bm{q}|), with the intrinsic parts ΠMLGvac=−g16q2/v2​q2+ξ2\Pi^{\rm MLG}_{\rm vac}=-\tfrac{g}{16}q^{2}/\sqrt{v^{2}q^{2}+\xi^{2}} (exact) and ΠvacBLG=−N0​ψ​(2​m​ξ/q2)\Pi^{\rm BLG}_{\rm vac}=-N_{0}\,\psi(2m\xi/q^{2}) computed numerically [N0=g​m/2​πN_{0}=gm/2\pi]. The dimensionless function ψ\psi is the interband bubble of the filled valence band in units of N0N_{0}, written in the scaled variables 𝒌=q​𝜿\bm{k}=q\bm{\kappa} and z=2​m​ξ/q2z=2m\xi/q^{2}:

ψ⁡(z)=1π​∫d2​κ​[1−cos⁡2​φ𝜿]​δ​(𝜿)z2+δ2​(𝜿),δ⁡(𝜿)=κ2+|𝜿+𝒆^|2,\psi(z)=\frac{1}{\pi}\int\!d^{2}\kappa\,\frac{\bigl[1-\cos 2\varphi_{\bm{\kappa}}\bigr]\,\delta(\bm{\kappa})}{z^{2}+\delta^{2}(\bm{\kappa})},\quad\delta(\bm{\kappa})=\kappa^{2}+|\bm{\kappa}+\hat{\bm{e}}|^{2}, (28)

where 𝒆^\hat{\bm{e}} is the unit vector along 𝒒\bm{q} and φ𝜿\varphi_{\bm{\kappa}} is the angle between 𝜿\bm{\kappa} and 𝜿+𝒆^\bm{\kappa}+\hat{\bm{e}}. The integral converges because the J=2J=2 coherence factor 1−cos⁡2​φ𝜿1-\cos 2\varphi_{\bm{\kappa}} vanishes as κ−2\kappa^{-2} at large κ\kappa; ψ⁡(0)=ln⁡4\psi(0)=\ln 4 reproduces the static intrinsic result [57], and ψ\psi decreases monotonically. The evaluation is checked against all limits on which the published results agree: the MLG static response [52], the hydrodynamic limit, the intrinsic-BLG constant N0​ln⁡4N_{0}\ln 4 [57], the compressibility sum rule Π(q→0,0)=−N0\Pi(q\to 0,0)=-N_{0} of doped BLG together with the known shape of its static response (flat, then a peak 1.75​N01.75N_{0} at q=2​kFq=2k_{F}, decaying to N0​ln⁡4N_{0}\ln 4) [57, 54], and ff-sum-rule tails. At this level, our results are consistent with those reported in Refs. [51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 49, 21, 45].

One technical point should be noted. The static limit of Eq. (27) contains principal-value structures at the Fermi-surface crossing angle and, for BLG only, at the backscattering configuration k=q/2k=q/2, θ=π\theta=\pi, where the J=2J=2 coherence factor is maximal, whereas the J=1J=1 factor of MLG vanishes. This is the same matrix-element structure responsible for the absence of backscattering suppression in BLG transport; numerically it makes the BLG bubble considerably harder to evaluate than the MLG one (Appendix C).

For doped graphene, the justification for using the RPA does not come from a small coupling constant: αg\alpha_{\rm g} is independent of density and can be of order unity. Rather, the approximation relies on the fourfold flavor degeneracy of graphene (N=g=4N=g=4), which makes the ring diagrams the leading contribution in a 1/N1/N expansion [58, 59, 60]. This provides the rationale for using the RPA even at αg∼0.5\alpha_{\rm g}\sim 0.5–22, as we do throughout this section.

VI.2 Doped monolayer graphene

Figure 2 shows the interlayer energy and capacitance correction for two parallel sheets of doped monolayer graphene. The behavior is qualitatively the same as for the electron gas. The energy crosses over from the bare second-order behavior to the plasmon zero-point law, now with ωp2​(q)=g​e2​μ​q/2​ϵ¯​ℏ2\omega_{p}^{2}(q)=ge^{2}\mu q/2\bar{\epsilon}\hbar^{2}, approached from below with a characteristic ∼15%\sim 15\% interband suppression around kF​d∼1k_{F}d\sim 1–22. The capacitance correction is positive at all separations studied (0.35≤kF​d≤600.35\leq k_{F}d\leq 60), with the closed asymptote

δ​Cinter−1=ℏ4​π​e2​n2​g​e2​μ2​ϵ¯​ℏ2​K1/2d5/2,K1/2=0.0198002,\delta C^{-1}_{\rm inter}=\frac{\hbar}{4\pi e^{2}n^{2}}\sqrt{\frac{ge^{2}\mu}{2\bar{\epsilon}\hbar^{2}}}\,\frac{K_{1/2}}{d^{5/2}},\qquad K_{1/2}=0.0198002, (29)

the γ=12\gamma=\tfrac{1}{2} member of a one-parameter family of constants KγK_{\gamma} obtained by repeating the zero-point analysis with ωp,ℓ2∝q​nℓγ\omega^{2}_{p,\ell}\propto q\,n_{\ell}^{\gamma} [Appendix B]; γ=12\gamma=\tfrac{1}{2} because ωp2∝μ∝n\omega_{p}^{2}\propto\mu\propto\sqrt{n} for Dirac carriers. The computed curvature reaches 0.990.99 of Eq. (29) by kF​d=30k_{F}d=30. The coefficient is smaller than the parabolic value K=K1K=K_{1} by the factor 2.42.4: the Dirac plasmon is less sensitive to density transfer. At n=1012n=10^{12} cm-2 and d=5.7d=5.7 nm the correction amounts to δ​dinter∗≃6.5×10−3\delta d^{*}_{\rm inter}\simeq 6.5\times 10^{-3} nm, about 0.2%0.2\% of the kinetic quantum-capacitance thickness of the two layers, with the characteristic scaling δC−1∝n−7/4d−5/2\delta C^{-1}\propto n^{-7/4}d^{-5/2}. Beyond the RPA, the long-wavelength plasmon weight of a Dirac liquid is not protected by Galilean invariance: the Drude weight DD is renormalized by interactions, D/D0≃1.1D/D_{0}\simeq 1.1–1.21.2 at αg∼0.5\alpha_{\rm g}\sim 0.5 and typical densities [61]. Since Eq. (29) depends on the plasmon weight only through μ\sqrt{\mu}, this correction is absorbed by μ→μ​D/D0\mu\to\mu D/D_{0} and shifts the asymptotic coefficient by 55–10%10\%; the constant K1/2K_{1/2} itself is unaffected.

VI.3 Doped bilayer graphene: interband suppression and sign reversal

Two parallel sheets of doped bilayer graphene behave differently from the electron gas despite the parabolic bands (Fig. 3). Three observations can be drawn from the numerical analysis described in Appendix C:

(i) Strong suppression. A control calculation for a fictitious four-flavor parabolic gas with the same mass, density, and interaction (BLG stripped of interband transitions and chirality factors) yields a positive curvature 3030–100100 times larger than the true two-band result over 0.5≤kF​d≤40.5\leq k_{F}d\leq 4. The BLG interlayer correction is the small residue of a near-cancellation driven by interband screening: even undoped BLG responds with the finite constant N0​ln⁡4N_{0}\ln 4 [57], so each sheet acts as an almost frequency-flat mirror, r→−1r\to-1, over a wide (q,ξ)(q,\xi) domain, and a capacitor formed by two nearly perfect mirrors has a Casimir energy nearly independent of the charge transfer.

(ii) Sign-reversal window. The residue changes sign twice: at kF​aB∗=1.25k_{F}a_{B}^{*}=1.25,

δ​(1/C)inter<0for0.55≲kF​d≲1.87,\delta(1/C)_{\rm inter}<0\quad\text{for}\quad 0.55\lesssim k_{F}d\lesssim 1.87, (30)

i.e., for 3​nm≲d≲113~\text{nm}\lesssim d\lesssim 11 nm at n=1012n=10^{12} cm-2, which is the range typical of experiments, interlayer correlations weakly enhance the capacitance of a BLG double layer, opposite in sign to the 2DEG and MLG results and obtained here already at ring level, without invoking excitonic physics. Outside the window the correction is positive and approaches the parabolic asymptote [Eq. (23) with the BLG mass] slowly (80%80\% at kF​d=60k_{F}d=60).

(iii) Smallness of the correction. In the window |δ​dinter∗|∼5×10−4|\delta d^{*}_{\rm inter}|\sim 5\times 10^{-4} nm at 101210^{12} cm-2: within the ring approximation, interlayer correlations are for practical purposes absent from the capacitance of doped BLG double layers.

One should keep in mind, however, that the residual identified in (i) is only about 1%1\% of the individual contributions that nearly cancel. Its value may therefore be affected by corrections beyond the two-band model, including the four-band structure at εF≳γ1/4\varepsilon_{F}\gtrsim\gamma_{1}/4, trigonal warping at very low energies, and, in particular, the gap induced by the displacement field generated by the charging itself [46, 12]. The two statements above have different status. The suppression requires only that the interband polarizability of BLG be comparable to the intraband one (N0​ln⁡4N_{0}\ln 4 versus N0N_{0}), which makes each sheet an almost frequency-independent mirror; this is a low-energy consequence of the chirality-two band contact and persists in the four-band model for εF≪γ1/4\varepsilon_{F}\ll\gamma_{1}/4, so the suppression is robust. The sign of the residue, by contrast, is decided by the balance of two nearly equal contributions and can be changed by perturbations of the spectrum at the percent level. The precise boundaries, and even the existence, of the sign window should therefore be regarded as two-band-model statements pending a four-band, self-consistently gapped calculation.

VI.4 Limits of validity near neutrality

The central formula, Eq. (14), relies on assumptions that become invalid as either layer approaches its neutrality point, a regime that capacitance experiments routinely probe.

(i) Loss of the controlled expansion. For the 2DEG the ring sum is exact as rs→0r_{s}\to 0. For MLG the coupling αg\alpha_{\rm g} is density independent, and screening weakens as qT​F=g​αg​kF→0q_{TF}=g\alpha_{\rm g}k_{F}\to 0; for BLG the effective rs∝1/kFr_{s}\propto 1/k_{F} diverges at neutrality. Below |n|∼1011|n|\sim 10^{11} cm-2 the ring approximation is uncontrolled.

(ii) Relative weight of the interlayer term. At fixed separation dd and decreasing density, the ratio of the interlayer correction to the kinetic quantum capacitance stays below the percent level for MLG down to kF​d≃0.1k_{F}d\simeq 0.1 (both quantities grow together as n→0n\to 0, ∝n−1/2\propto n^{-1/2}), whereas for BLG, whose kinetic term is density independent, the ratio grows monotonically as n→0n\to 0. No small parameter justifies a description of BLG double layers near neutrality in terms of single-layer quantities alone.

(iii) The excitonic channel. The capacitance curvature displaces the system to (n¯+δ​n,n¯−δ​n)(\bar{n}+\delta n,\bar{n}-\delta n); at double neutrality n¯=0\bar{n}=0 this is an electron-hole double layer, whose interlayer particle-particle channel is the pairing channel of exciton condensation [62, 63, 64], observed in quantum-Hall double bilayers and in strongly enhanced interlayer tunneling at total neutrality [65, 66]. Near the condensation the imbalance curvature acquires a negative contribution that rings miss entirely (in the language of Ref. [23], the interlayer polarizability diverges for bound interlayer pairs): the capacitance at double neutrality is an order-parameter susceptibility, not a density-of-states measurement. Equation (14) fails there for the same reason Lifshitz theory fails for chemically bonding surfaces.

(iv) Disorder. Electron–hole puddles smear |n|≲1010|n|\lesssim 10^{10}–101110^{11} cm-2 [11].

(v) BLG band-structure limits. Two-band validity requires εF≪γ1/4\varepsilon_{F}\ll\gamma_{1}/4; trigonal warping invalidates the J=2J=2 chirality at meV scales; and the charging field gaps the spectrum.

VII Discussion: limiting regimes, prior results, and the crossover

We now summarize the behavior of δ​Cinter−1\delta C^{-1}_{\rm inter} across the bilayer phase diagram, focusing on the two limiting regimes where controlled results are available and discuss the crossover between them.

(i) High density (this work). The second-order functions G,HG,H at κ​d≲1\kappa d\lesssim 1 are controlled for rs≪1r_{s}\ll 1, and the plasmon zero-point asymptote (23) at κ​d≫1\kappa d\gg 1 is exact at leading order in 1/κ​d1/\kappa d for any rsr_{s} (Sec. V.3). The sign is positive: the correction is carried by the particle-hole (plasmon) channel, and transferring charge weakens the van der Waals binding, which is maximal at equal densities.

(ii) Low density. The opposite limit is classical and well understood. The line of thought goes back to Bello, Levin, Shklovskii, and Efros [5] and to Chenskii and Tkach [6], who showed that Coulomb correlations among localized surface charges produce a negative effective density of states in capacitance. This was the earliest example of correlation-dominated capacitance and the conceptual ancestor of the negative compressibility measured in Refs. [67, 3, 4]. For a dilute double layer, rs≫1r_{s}\gg 1 and n​d2≲1nd^{2}\lesssim 1, the electrons form interpenetrating Wigner-crystal-like configurations; a transferred electron remains bound to the correlation hole it leaves behind, and the resulting electron-hole dipoles resist charging only through their weak mutual repulsion. The capacitance is then anomalously large, d∗→0d^{*}\to 0 [19], consistent with the large enhancement observed in Ref. [25]; equivalently, the interlayer contribution to 1/C1/C is large and negative, cancelling most of the geometric term. Even at equal densities the correlation hole is visible in the energetics: when each electron faces a depleted disk in the opposite layer, the interlayer energy grows linearly with dd, Eint​(d)/𝒜≃Eint​(0)/𝒜+2​π​e2​n1​n2​d/ϵ¯E_{\rm int}(d)/\mathcal{A}\simeq E_{\rm int}(0)/\mathcal{A}+2\pi e^{2}n_{1}n_{2}d/\bar{\epsilon}, the electrostatic energy of a double layer of correlation holes. [For a fixed interlayer pair correlation g12​(r)g_{12}(r) and d≪n−1/2d\ll n^{-1/2} the linear term is exactly (2​π​e2/ϵ¯)​n1​n2​[1−g12​(0)]​d(2\pi e^{2}/\bar{\epsilon})\,n_{1}n_{2}[1-g_{12}(0)]\,d, since ∫d2r[(r2+d2)−1/2−r−1]=−2πd\int d^{2}r\,[(r^{2}+d^{2})^{-1/2}-r^{-1}]=-2\pi d]. This is the microscopic origin of the capacitance enhancement: with n1​n2=n¯2−δ​n2n_{1}n_{2}=\bar{n}^{2}-\delta n^{2} its curvature ∂δ​n2\partial^{2}_{\delta n} equals −4πe2d/ϵ¯-4\pi e^{2}d/\bar{\epsilon} and cancels the geometric term of Eq. (3) identically, so the d∗→0d^{*}\to 0 of Ref. [19] follows exactly in the correlation-hole picture. The variational treatment of gate-screened layers [20] and the bilayer Wigner-crystal phase diagram [68] refine this limit.

(iii) The crossover. The sign of δ​Cinter−1\delta C^{-1}_{\rm inter} must therefore change along a line in the (rs,kF​d)(r_{s},k_{F}d) plane. In diagrammatic language this is a competition between the particle-hole channel (rings; positive contribution, dominant at high density) and the particle-particle channel (interlayer excitons and dipoles; negative contribution, dominant at low density). These are the two mechanisms identified at lowest order in the cross-quantum-capacitance analysis of Berthod et al. [23], now supported by controlled calculations in both limits. Their perturbative treatment of the particle–particle channel produces a logarithmic singularity at equal layer densities, the weak-coupling signature of a two-dimensional interlayer bound state; the singularity is cut by the exponentially small exciton binding energy, which is why this channel is weak, and the ring result controlled, at high density. In our view, locating the sign-change line is the most concrete problem that this physics poses for quantum Monte Carlo: it requires E⁡(n¯+δ​n,n¯−δ​n,d)E(\bar{n}+\delta n,\bar{n}-\delta n;d) to order δ​n2\delta n^{2} at a handful of (rs,kF​d)(r_{s},k_{F}d) points, an imbalance-resolved bilayer calculation that existing bilayer QMC data (taken at fixed equal densities or fixed polarization [69, 47]) do not provide. The Singwi-Tosi-Land-Sjölander treatment of interlayer local fields [70, 71, 72], benchmarked at small rsr_{s} against the exact H⁡(x)H(x), is the natural interpolation tool in the meantime; Hartree-Fock studies of double layers [73] capture the exchange-driven part of the crossover.

(iv) BLG anomaly. Bilayer graphene falls outside this classification: there the ring contribution itself is suppressed by interband screening and reverses sign in the accessible window, Eq. (30). For experiments of the type of Refs. [9, 12, 14] the implication is that interpreting BLG double-layer capacitance in terms of single-layer compressibilities alone is quantitatively safe at doped densities. This is not because interlayer correlations are weak, but because the dispersion energy of two nearly perfect mirrors is insensitive to their charge dynamics.

(v) Drag-capacitance correspondence. Drag and the Casimir compressibility are two moments of the same interlayer fluctuation spectrum (Sec. IV.3). Within the ring approximation both follow from the same screened interlayer propagator, so a model that fits the measured drag [1, 74] predicts δ​Cinter−1\delta C^{-1}_{\rm inter} with no adjustable parameters. Near the exciton instability both quantities become anomalous together, perfect drag [2, 65] and the capacitance anomaly of Sec. VI.4; formulating exact sum rules linking the two is an open problem.

(vi) Experimental outlook. The interlayer correction carries a parameter-free signature: δC−1inter∝n−3/2d−5/2\delta C^{-1}_{\rm inter}\propto n^{-3/2}d^{-5/2} with coefficient (23) for parabolic layers, and n−7/4d−5/2n^{-7/4}d^{-5/2} with coefficient (29) for MLG. It is separable from the geometric term (density independent, ∝d\propto d) and from the single-layer compressibilities (dd independent, directly measurable in the penetration-field geometry [3, 4]) by varying nn at several fixed dd in one heterostructure family. The predicted magnitudes are small: at the percent level of d∗d^{*} in GaAs double wells, and 10−310^{-3} of the single-layer quantum capacitance in graphene at 101210^{12} cm-2. Two points bear on their observability. First, the geometric term is not a background of unknown size: dd is measured independently, and capacitance spectroscopy of correlations, from the negative compressibility of Refs. [3, 4] onward, has consisted of resolving percent-level shifts of d∗d^{*} against it, while modern techniques resolve considerably smaller relative signals [14, 15]. Second, the interlayer term is the only contribution to d∗d^{*} that depends on nn and dd jointly, so a family of devices at several dd, or the penetration-field geometry at fixed dd and several nn, isolates it without a subtraction model. In this sense it is, like Coulomb drag, determined exclusively by interlayer correlations: it vanishes identically without them. The effect grows rapidly toward low density and small kF​dk_{F}d, where the crossover physics discussed above takes over. A measurement of δ​dinter∗\delta d^{*}_{\rm inter} would constitute a thermodynamic detection of a dispersion force.

VIII Summary

We have developed a theory of the interlayer-correlation contribution to the quantum capacitance of electron double layers. The main results are as follows.

(1) Within the functional-integral (RPA) framework, the separation-dependent part of the bilayer ground-state energy is exactly the nonretarded Lifshitz energy of two conducting sheets, Eqs. (14)–(16), with reflection amplitudes built from the layer polarizabilities. The interlayer capacitance correction, Eq. (5), is the second density derivative of this dispersion energy (a Casimir compressibility). Retardation is negligible for all capacitor geometries; the zero-point modes are the coupled plasmons of the bilayer.

(2) For the 2DEG double layer the high-density limit is solved: the interlayer second-order energy is infrared finite (no Gell-Mann-Brueckner resummation is forced in two dimensions) and defines universal functions G⁡(kF​d)G(k_{F}d), H⁡(kF​d)H(k_{F}d); at κ​d≫1\kappa d\gg 1 the ring sum is dominated by plasmon zero-point motion and yields the closed asymptotes (22) and (23) with universal constants J=−0.0629780J=-0.0629780 and K=0.0477118K=0.0477118, the former reproducing the quantum-well dispersion energy of Ref. [41] to all quoted digits. The sign is proven positive: at high density, interlayer correlations oppose charging. The mixed-derivative (cross) term is only one third of the effect.

(3) For graphene: doped monolayers behave like the electron gas with K1/2=0.0198002K_{1/2}=0.0198002; doped bilayer graphene is anomalous, interband screening suppresses the interlayer correction by one to two orders of magnitude and, within the two-band model, reverses its sign in the window 0.55≲kF​d≲1.90.55\lesssim k_{F}d\lesssim 1.9, Eq. (30). The suppression is robust; the sign window is a two-band-model result whose boundaries, and existence, are sensitive to the displacement-field gap and to trigonal warping (Sec. VI.3).

(4) The theory has well-defined limits of validity. Upon dilution the particle–particle (interlayer-exciton) channel, absent from the ring diagrams, grows and acts in the opposite sense, making the correction large and negative [19, 25]; a line in the (rs,kF​d)(r_{s},k_{F}d) plane must therefore separate capacitance reduction from capacitance enhancement. No resummation is controlled in its vicinity, and we pose the location of this sign-change line as a concrete target for imbalance-resolved bilayer quantum Monte Carlo. The end point of this evolution is reached in electron-hole double layers beyond the exciton-condensation transition: the transferred charge then measures the equation of state of the dipolar exciton fluid, e2​δ​C−1=∂μex/∂nexe^{2}\delta C^{-1}=\partial\mu_{\rm ex}/\partial n_{\rm ex}, and d∗d^{*} collapses from ≈d{\approx}\,d to ∼d2/aex{\sim}\,d^{2}/a_{\rm ex}, set by the dipole-dipole repulsion (aexa_{\rm ex} is the interexciton spacing). The quantum Hall counterpart of this collapse, d∗≃0.6​d2/ℓBd^{*}\simeq 0.6\,d^{2}/\ell_{B}, was conjectured as an experimental signature of exciton condensation in graphene double layers in a strong magnetic field [75]; the growth of the negative correction on approach to the transition, the ladder channel nearing its pole, is its equilibrium precursor, and the character of the anomaly at the transition itself (jump versus fluctuation peak) reflects the order of the transition.

Beyond the specific results, the Lifshitz form of the interlayer energy connects the capacitance problem to the asymptotic benchmarks of dispersion-force theory [35, 39, 44], and Eq. (26) relates the interlayer capacitance correction to the Casimir pressure between the layers with a universal coefficient.

Appendix C Numerical methods and validation

All integrals were evaluated with Gauss–Legendre quadratures; momentum grids concentrate nodes at small qq with qmax=16/2​d+4​kFq_{\max}=16/2d+4k_{F}, and frequencies are mapped by ξ=Ωc​tan⁡t\xi=\Omega_{c}\tan t. Capacitance curvatures are central second differences along (n+δ​n,n−δ​n)(n+\delta n,n-\delta n) with steps δ​n/n=0.02\delta n/n=0.02–0.050.05 and quadrature grids frozen across the stencil (removing the dominant noise source); results are stable under step halving and grid doubling at the 10−310^{-3} level or better.

2DEG. Validation: the closed-form Lindhard function against direct numerical integration (≲2×10−3\lesssim 2\times 10^{-3}, limited by the reference); rsr_{s} independence of E2/NE_{2}/N at fixed kF​dk_{F}d (machine precision); the analytic constants c0=2−π/2c_{0}=2-\pi/2 and Eq. (24); convergence onto Eqs. (22) and (23) (Fig. 1).

Graphene. The bubbles (27) are tabulated on universal grids in (q/kF,ξ/vF​q)(q/k_{F},\ \xi/v_{F}q) (200×160200\times 160, cubic interpolation) with three singular structures handled explicitly: (a) the Fermi-surface crossing angle (principal value as ξ→0\xi\to 0), integrated with log-spaced node pairs symmetric about the crossing so the singular parts cancel pointwise; (b) the backscattering endpoint θ=π\theta=\pi (BLG only; the MLG coherence factor removes it); (c) a second, radial principal-value structure at k=q/2k=q/2, where rows on either side diverge as ±1/(k−q/2)\pm 1/(k-q/2), integrated with paired log-spaced nodes symmetric about q/2q/2. Omitting (b) or (c) produces O⁡(1)O(1) errors in the BLG static limit, while the MLG case, which is less sensitive to them, appears correct; the validation suite of Sec. VI.1 catches both.
